entities.name: Marie, Prioress of Poissy
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marie of France (1393–1438), a princess of the House of Valois and daughter of King Charles VI and Queen Isabeau of Bavaria, served as Prioress of the Royal Monastery of Poissy from 1408 until her death. Her life, largely confined within the walls of this prestigious Dominican convent, exemplifies the intricate intersection of royal piety, dynastic strategy, and the role of high-born women in late medieval French monasticism. Her tenure as prioress unfolded against the tumultuous backdrop of the Hundred Years' War and the Armagnac-Burgundian civil conflict, positioning her as a quiet yet significant figure in the religious and social history of a deeply fractured kingdom.

Entering the Dominican convent of Poissy, historically founded by King Saint Louis IX, at the tender age of four in 1397, Marie's monastic path was set early, driven by a combination of spiritual devotion and royal custom. She took her solemn vows in 1408, the same year she was elected Prioress, assuming leadership over a community of aristocratic nuns. This position bestowed considerable administrative and spiritual authority, requiring her to manage the convent's extensive estates, oversee its finances, and maintain the spiritual discipline of the order. During her leadership, the monastery, a traditional royal necropolis and retreat, faced direct threats and economic hardship due to the widespread warfare and political instability that gripped France.
